newsitem.title: USA: Foster Wheeler temporarily closes Robbins.
newsitem.headline: Foster Wheeler temporarily closes Robbins.

text.p: Foster Wheeler Corp on Wednesday was forced to temporarily shut down its Robbins incinerator in Illinois after a construction permit ran out, officials at Foster Wheeler and the Illinois Environmental Protection Agency said Friday.
"The construction permit covers the construction and this 180-day initial start-up period, after which they need an operating permit," Illinois EPA spokesman Dennis McMurray said.
June 2 is the deadline for the agency decision on whether to grant the incinerator an operating permit, McMurray said.

"The agency has issued a draft permit proposing to grant a permit, but there is a public comment period running until May 27 for written comments and there's always the possibility that the public may raise an issue that we feel needs to be addressed."

Thomas O'Brien, a senior vice president and general counsel at Foster Wheeler, said while June 3 would be the first day Robbins could re-ignite the boilers, the facility will continue to accept waste, operating essentially as a transfer station.

"We kind of expected it," O'Brien said. "The construction start-up permit, we were operating under that, which is a temporary thing. And we completed the 180 days under that permit, but unfortunately the timing was such that we have this 24, 25 day gap."
O'Brien said Foster Wheeler will use the down time to perform some preventive maintenance and make enhancements to the facility.
"It will not be a financial burden," he said.
Last month legislation to restore a state subsidy to two bond-financed waste-to-energy incinerators -- one of them Robbins -- failed on the third reading in the Illinois House of Representatives.
The subsidy's repeal has imperiled more than $500 million of tax-exempt, unrated bonds that were sold for three projects, including $320 million of debt for the Robbins project.

The EPA's McMurray the Illinois Pollution Control Board met in an emergency session Friday to consider Foster Wheeler's request to continue to accept waste from the 12 municipalities that they have contracts with. The EPA recommended that the request should be granted, albeit with several additional conditions.

"I have heard that they have approved it effective today," McMurray said. "So it means that they can start receiving waste again but they can not burn it or store it. They can sort it and ship it off to other places."
